## Introduction

`miaTime` is a package in the `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("mia")` family, providing
tools for time series manipulation using the
`r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("TreeSummarizedExperiment")` data container.

## Installation

`miaTime` is hosted on Bioconductor, and can be installed using via
`BiocManager`.

```{r}
#| label: install
#| eval: false

BiocManager::install("miaTime")
```

## Load the package

Once installed, `miaTime` is made available in the usual way.

```{r}
#| label: load_package

library(miaTime)
```

## Divergence between time points

Divergence refers to the quantification of dissimilarity or difference between 
microbiome samples taken at different time points. This concept is crucial for 
tracking how microbial communities change or evolve over time, either in 
individuals or experimental conditions.

### Types of divergence provided

`miaTime` provides several functions for calculating divergences:

 - Baseline divergence: Measures the dissimilarity between each sample and a 
 reference (typically the first time point) within a group (such as per subject).

 - Stepwise (rolling) divergence: Assesses the change between consecutive (or 
 defined interval) time points by comparing each sample to the previous ith
 sample in the series.
 
The divergence is typically calculated using a beta diversity metric, such as 
Bray-Curtis dissimilarity, which quantifies how different two communities are 
in terms of their composition.

For rolling or stepwise divergences, the calculation measures how much the 
community shifts from one sampling point to the next.

### Purpose

Quantifying divergence allows researchers to:

- Track temporal instability or stability of the microbiome.

- Compare change rates between individuals or treatments.

- Identify significant shifts or stable periods in the microbiome composition.

### Practical application

For example, in a human gut microbiome time series, calculating divergence helps 
determine how resistant the microbial ecosystem is to perturbations (such as 
antibiotics or diet changes) and how long it takes to return (if at all) to 
its original state.

Divergences can be calculated with `*Divergence()` functions. In the example
below, we use a subset of the HMP2 inflammatory bowel disease cohort, where
each subject was sampled before and after treatment. For each subject, we
compare the follow-up sample to the first sample.

```{r}
#| label: base_divergence

data(HMP_2019_ibdmdb)
tse <- HMP_2019_ibdmdb

tse <- addBaselineDivergence(
    tse,
    time.col = "days_from_first_collection",
    group = "subject_id",
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray")
```

The results are stored in `colData`. Divergence is zero for the baseline
samples, so we compare the follow-up samples between IBD subtypes.

```{r}
#| label: base_divergence_plot

library(miaViz)
library(ggplot2)

plotBoxplot(
    tse[, tse[["time_diff"]] > 0],
    col.var = "divergence",
    x = "disease_subtype") +
    labs(x = "IBD subtype", y = "Bray-Curtis divergence from baseline")
```

Stepwise divergence compares each sample to the previous sample of the same
subject. In `hitchip1006`, some subjects have up to five samples.

```{r}
#| label: time_divergence

data(hitchip1006)
tse <- hitchip1006
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")

res <- getStepwiseDivergence(
    tse,
    time.col = "time",
    group = "subject",
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    method = "bray")
res[!is.na(res[["divergence"]]), ] |> head()
```

The `time_diff` column shows how much time separates each sample from the one
it is compared to. The intervals vary between subjects, which is worth keeping
in mind when comparing divergences.

## Short term change

Short term change measures how the abundance of each feature changes between
consecutive time points. `getShortTermChange()` returns the absolute change,
growth rate and rate of change for each feature (Ji et al. 2020). Below, we
use `minimalgut`, a time series of a synthetic gut community in bioreactors.

```{r}
#| label: short_term_change

data(minimalgut)
tse <- minimalgut
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")

df <- getShortTermChange(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    time.col = "Time.hr",
    group = "StudyIdentifier")
df |> head()
```

## Stability

Intermediate stability (Lahti et al. 2014) relates the change of a feature
between consecutive time points to how far it was from a reference point,
by default its median abundance. See `?getStability` for the formulas.

```{r}
#| label: stability

tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "rclr")
tse <- addStability(
    tse,
    assay.type = "rclr",
    time.col = "Time.hr",
    group = "StudyIdentifier")
rowData(tse)[, grepl("stability", colnames(rowData(tse))), drop = FALSE] |>
    head()
```

## Bimodality

The coefficient of bimodality tells whether the abundance of a feature has
two modes, for instance high in some time points and rare in others. Together
with abundance, it can be used to find conditionally rare taxa (Shade et al.
2014). Below, we use one vessel of an artificial gut time series.

```{r}
#| label: bimodality

data(SilvermanAGutData)
tse <- SilvermanAGutData
tse <- tse[, tse[["Vessel"]] == 1]
# Remove samples without any counts, as their relative abundances are undefined
tse <- tse[, colSums(assay(tse, "counts")) > 0]
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")

tse <- addBimodality(tse, assay.type = "relabundance")
bimodal <- rownames(tse)[which(rowData(tse)[["bimodality"]] > 0.95)]
abundant <- getAbundant(
    tse, assay.type = "relabundance", abundant.th = 0.5/100)
intersect(bimodal, abundant)
```

## Visualize time series

We can visualize time series data with `r BiocStyle::Biocpkg("miaViz")`. Below,
we visualize the five most abundant taxa in one bioreactor of `minimalgut`.

```{r}
#| label: plot_series

library(miaViz)

tse <- minimalgut
tse <- tse[, tse[["StudyIdentifier"]] == "Bioreactor A"]
tse <- transformAssay(tse, method = "relabundance")

p <- plotSeries(
    tse,
    assay.type = "relabundance",
    time.col = "Time.hr",
    features = getTop(tse, 5),
    colour.by = "rownames")
p
```
